newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Swine fever speads to fourth Dutch province.
newsitem.headline: Swine fever speads to fourth Dutch province.

text.p: A swine fever epidemic raging in the south of the Netherlands had spread to a fourth new area -- the eastern province of Overijssel, the Dutch farm ministry said on Wednesday.
The highly contagious pig disease has been detected at 366 farms so far and is showing few signs of abating.
It broke out in North Brabant in February this year, spreading quickly to neighbouring Limburg and then last month to the province of Gelderland in the east.
A ministry spokeswoman said an investigation was underway to find out how the disease, which is not harmful to humans, found its way to Overijssel despite strict livestock transport bans.
"Swine fever has been discovered on one farm and we are investigating the other farms in the area," the spokewoman said.
A ban on transporting livestock in an area 20 kilometres around the farm has been imposed, meaning the country's biggest cattle market at nearby Zwolle will have to close temprorarily.
Operations are being moved to the central city of Utrecht.
"The area has to be screened and while this is happening, the market cannot be allowed," the spokeswoman said, adding this could take up to two weeks.
The whole epidemic has involved the slaughter of more than five million pigs and cost an estimated 1.6 billion guilders so far. Most of the bill has been paid by the European Union.
The disease has also cost billions of guilders in lost trade.

The export of live pigs is banned from the whole country and exports of pork from infected areas are also barred. In addition many countries including the United States have imposed their own bans on imports of live pigs and pork from the Netherlands.
The cost of the outbreak has prompted the EU to criticise Dutch intensive farming methods and led to plans for a radical shake-up of the entire sector next year.
Last month Guy Legras, director general for agriculture at the European Commission, said the epidemic was evidence that intensive farming must be re-examined.

"I think the Netherlands, which has been the champion of intensification, realises today that we are in a position where half the country is closed off and the crisis continues to spread," he told a news conference on EU farm reform.
Dutch farm minister Jozias van Aartsen in July announced a blueprint for reforming the sector, entailing a 25 percent cut in pig numbers and more environmentally friendly production methods.
Before the start of the outbreak, there were around 14 million pigs in the Netherlands.
